subtype: Managing Anger, Envy & Ego at Work
passage: At the cooperative sugar factory near Kolhapur, Pradeep had trained Indu when she joined. Two years later she was made shift supervisor, not him. He heard it at the tea stall and felt his face burn. That evening he snapped at his younger brother over nothing. At night he lay awake, thinking of every mistake she'd ever made. The next morning he nearly skipped her first meeting. Instead he went, sat at the back and said little. Afterward he walked by the cane fields and admitted to himself that she was good at planning, better than him. He congratulated her the next day, stiffly. She said, "You taught me half of it." His chest loosened a little.

passage: Rosa had worked at the Lima architecture firm longer than Bao, but it was Bao's design the partners chose for the library project. In the meeting, Rosa smiled and clapped. In the bathroom afterward, she gripped the sink and breathed. She wanted to point out, loudly, that his design ignored drainage. Instead, she waited until the next morning, calmer. She wrote Bao a short message: "Congrats. One thing to check, the drainage on the east side might flood in heavy rain. Happy to help." Bao replied, "You're right, I missed that. Can we look together?" They spent an afternoon on it. Rosa still felt a pinch when the partners praised him. But the building would be better.

Hi Karthik,
I owe you an apology for Thursday's meeting. When your promotion was announced, I congratulated you in two words and then shot down your first proposal harder than it deserved. That wasn't about the proposal. Honestly, I was envious. We joined in the same month, and I'd been telling myself the role was mine. I went home angry, mostly at myself. I've thought about it since. You led the vendor migration when no one else wanted it, and you did it well. I can learn from that. I'd still like to discuss my concerns about the budget line, calmly this time, maybe on Monday? And I'll say it properly now: congratulations. You earned it.
Asif

subtype: Managing Anger, Envy & Ego at Work
passage: Jeevan, you asked about my worst ego moment at work. Easy. Last year, on a client call, our intern, just twenty-one, interrupted me: 'Sorry, Anirban sir, that figure is wrong.' In front of the client. I felt heat go up my neck. I actually opened my mouth to say, 'Let's take that offline,' which would have meant: be quiet. Then I looked at the sheet. She was right. So I said, 'Good catch, thank you; the correct number is what she said.' The client smiled. After the call I walked around the block because I was still angry, and not really at her. At myself for being wrong, and at the feeling of being shown up. When I came back I told her the catch was great, and that next time she could message me privately first. She did, from then on.

qa.q: What did the intern point out during the client call?
qa.a: That Anirban's figure was wrong.

qa.q: What did the heat going up Anirban's neck show about how he felt?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and threatened, his ego stung at being corrected in front of a client.

qa.q: What did Anirban do that kept things professional?
qa.a: He checked the sheet, thanked her publicly, cooled off with a walk, and later gave her private guidance on how to raise such issues.

qa.q: How might the intern have felt when Anirban thanked her?
qa.a: Relieved and respected, since she had taken a risk correcting a senior in front of a client.

subtype: Managing Anger, Envy & Ego at Work
passage: I'm Vasudha. I sat across from Tejas the morning the promotion email came. The team lead post went to Kunal, who had joined a year after Tejas. I watched Tejas read the email, go very still, and close his laptop. He walked out for twenty minutes. When he came back he was red around the eyes, but he went straight to Kunal's desk and said, "Congratulations. You'll be good at it." I couldn't tell you what he felt. In the team meeting that afternoon, when Kunal presented the new plan, Tejas asked two sharp questions, and I tensed. But they were fair questions, and then he offered to take the hardest client. A week later he booked a meeting with our manager; I heard he asked, "What would I have needed to show?" He didn't sulk in the pantry the way some of us would have. I'm still not sure how he did it.

qa.q: Who got the team lead post?

qa.a: Tejas was probably hurt and envious, maybe angry, and stepped away to calm down before reacting.

qa.a: Taking time out, congratulating Kunal, asking fair questions, volunteering for the hardest client, and asking the manager what he would need to show.

Monday. At the all-hands, the director praised Deepika's client pitch by name, twice. Asif, who had built half the slides, clapped and felt his jaw lock. At lunch he said to a colleague, "Nice to present other people's work." It came out uglier than he meant.
Thursday. Deepika stopped by his desk. "Someone told me what you said. I did mention your slides to the director. She just didn't repeat it." Asif's face burned. He mumbled something, and she left. That night he couldn't sleep. The truth was he wanted to be seen, and he had never once asked to present.
Two weeks later. Asif asked his manager if he could present the next pitch. He also apologised to Deepika properly, over coffee, without excuses. She said, "Want to co-present? I'll take questions, you take the numbers." The pitch went well. When the director praised them both, he noticed his jaw stayed loose.

subtype: Managing Anger, Envy & Ego at Work
passage: Farida, you're angry that the new girl got the conference slot. Let old Ramesh Uncle tell you about Joseph. When I was twenty-six at the railway coach workshop in Perambur, Joseph joined as a junior, sharp as a blade. Within a year the chief engineer asked Joseph, not me, to lead the new coach design. I was furious. I told everyone Joseph was a flatterer. I stopped sharing my calculations with him. For six months the project limped, because he needed load figures only I had. Then one night the chief called us both in and said, "Work together, or you're both off it." I went home ashamed; I knew I had been hurting the work to hurt him. Next morning I brought Joseph my notebooks. We finished eight weeks late, but that coach ran for thirty years, and we became friends. So feel the anger, Farida. Then ask whether it's feeding the work or eating it.

qa.q: Where did Ramesh work at twenty-six?
qa.a: At the railway coach workshop in Perambur.

qa.q: What was young Ramesh feeling when Joseph was chosen to lead?
qa.a: Ramesh felt furious and envious at being passed over for a junior.

qa.q: What was Ramesh's turning point, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Bringing Joseph the notebooks after the chief's warning; it put the work above his ego and let the project finish.

qa.q: How might Joseph have experienced those six months?
qa.a: Joseph was probably frustrated and isolated, blocked from figures he needed and hearing himself called a flatterer.

subtype: Managing Anger, Envy & Ego at Work
passage:
The promotion email arrived at four: Lakshmi would be head chef. Aadhya read it twice on the kitchen tablet, then put it face down.

At six, a 300-plate wedding order was due, and two cooks had called in sick.

Aadhya's jaw ached from clenching. She had been at the hotel a year longer. She had trained Lakshmi on the tandoor. Lakshmi walked in, saw her face, and hesitated.

For a moment Aadhya wanted to say something cutting. Instead she went into the cold store, stood among the crates for sixty seconds, and breathed.

When she came out, she said, "Congratulations. Tell me where you want me tonight."

Lakshmi looked relieved. "Can you run the grill line? You're faster than me there."

They got the order out by nine. Afterwards, Aadhya wrote a note to herself: ask the manager what I need for the next opening. Then she went home and cried in the auto, which was allowed.

qa.q: How many plates was the wedding order?
qa.a: It was a 300-plate wedding order.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when she read the promotion email?
qa.a: Aadhya felt envious and angry, clenching her jaw, because she had more experience and had trained Lakshmi.

qa.q: Which choice helped Aadhya handle her anger professionally?
qa.a: Stepping into the cold store to breathe for sixty seconds before speaking, then offering help, stopped her from saying something cutting.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi have felt when she saw Aadhya's face?
qa.a: Lakshmi was probably uneasy and worried about resentment, which is why she hesitated and then looked relieved at the congratulations.

grounding: Under a busy wedding order, a young chef manages envy and anger after a colleague's promotion and stays professional.

At the Monday all-hands in the Bengaluru office, the director called out Shreya's name for the quarterly award. Shreya had joined eight months ago. Chandrika had been there three years.

Chandrika clapped. Her face felt stiff. On the way back to her desk, she caught herself composing a message to a friend: "Some people just know how to show off." She deleted it.

That evening she made herself look honestly at what Shreya had done: rebuilt the client dashboard, presented it herself to the director, sent a summary to the whole team. Chandrika had done similar work, but quietly.

The envy was still there. But under it was something useful.

On Tuesday she stopped by Shreya's desk. "Congratulations. That dashboard was really good. Would you show me how you set up the director review?"

Shreya blinked, then smiled widely. "Of course. Honestly, I was nervous you'd be annoyed."

"I was, a bit," Chandrika admitted. "I'm working on it."

qa.a: Chandrika had been there three years.

qa.a: Chandrika felt envious and a bit resentful that a newer colleague won the award, even though she clapped.

qa.a: She deleted the bitter message, looked honestly at what Shreya did differently, and asked Shreya to teach her, turning rivalry into learning.

qa.a: Shreya had been nervous that Chandrika would be annoyed, and after Tuesday she felt relieved and pleased to be asked for help.

"You corrected me in front of the client," Wasim said, closing the meeting room door. His voice was level, but his ears were red.

Deepika looked up. "The figure was wrong."

"It was. And I'd have fixed it. But saying 'that's not right, Wasim' in front of them made me look like I don't know my own numbers."

"I was worried they'd notice first."

"Fair. Can we agree on something? If you spot an error during a call, message me, and I'll correct it myself. If it's urgent, say 'let me add one detail' and fix it."

Deepika was quiet. "I didn't think about how it looked. I'm sorry."

"I'm sorry I went silent for the rest of the meeting. That didn't help either."

"You were sulking."

Wasim laughed despite himself. "I was sulking. I was angry for about an hour."

"And now?"

"Now I want us to look good in front of clients. Both of us."

When Irfan got the team lead role, I was sure it should've been me. I'd been there longer. I'd trained him. At the announcement I clapped and smiled, and then went to the stairwell and punched the railing. My knuckles hurt for a week.
For a month I was petty. I took extra time replying to his messages. I rolled my eyes in meetings. I told myself I wasn't jealous, just "honest".
Then my old mentor asked me, "What do you want: to be right, or to grow?" I didn't like the question.
I asked my manager, directly, why I hadn't been chosen. The answer stung: Irfan brought people together; I did great work alone. It was true.
I apologised to Irfan for the eye-rolling. He was gracious. Now I'm working on the thing he's better at. I'm Eshaan, and my knuckles are fine now.

qa.q: What did Eshaan punch in the stairwell?
qa.a: The railing.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel when Irfan got the role?
qa.a: Eshaan felt envious and angry, sure the role should have been Eshaan's, though outwardly smiling.

qa.q: What turned Eshaan's envy into something useful?
qa.a: Asking the manager directly why, accepting the honest answer, apologising, and working on the skill Irfan had.

qa.q: How might Irfan have experienced the month of pettiness?
qa.a: Irfan probably felt hurt and awkward, sensing resentment from someone who had trained him.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional handling envy and ego after a rival's promotion and responding maturely.

Manager's note. Suraj, sales team lead.
In Tuesday's review, the regional head praised the new client deal and credited Ananya's presentation. Kishore had found the client and done most of the groundwork. I saw his face tighten. After the meeting he typed fast in the team chat, then deleted it.
He came to me an hour later, visibly angry. "My work, her name." I let him say it. Then I asked what he wanted to happen.
He thought, and said he wanted his role on the record, not to embarrass Ananya. We agreed he'd send a short note to the regional head summarising the deal timeline with everyone's parts listed, and I'd add a line confirming it.
He did it calmly. Ananya, to her credit, replied-all thanking him for the groundwork.
I've noted that I should have named everyone's contributions in the meeting myself. I will next time.

qa.q: Whose presentation did the regional head credit?
qa.a: Ananya's presentation.

qa.q: What does Kishore typing fast and then deleting suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Kishore felt angry and hurt, tempted to lash out, but held back.

qa.q: How did Suraj help Kishore handle the status threat professionally?
qa.a: Suraj let him vent, asked what he wanted, and helped him record his contribution calmly without attacking Ananya.

qa.q: How might Ananya have felt when Kishore's note went out?
qa.a: Ananya might have felt a bit embarrassed but relieved it was handled fairly, which is why she thanked him.

grounding: Shows a young professional managing anger over lost credit with a manager's help and handling it professionally.

Wednesday night
Aparna here. Irfan presented "his" idea in the product meeting today. It was the idea I'd shared with him over lunch last week. Everyone loved it.
I wanted to scream. I sat there smiling, then cried in the washroom.
Then I made myself wait before doing anything. I went for a walk, texted my sister, ate dinner.
Tonight, calmer, I wrote down what I actually want: credit, yes, but also to keep working with Irfan without a war.
Plan for tomorrow: talk to him privately. "The idea you presented came from our lunch. I'd like us to present the next steps together." If he refuses, I'll take it to my manager with the chat where I first described it.
Also: I'll write my ideas down before sharing them over lunch from now on. Lesson learned.

qa.q: Where had Aparna first shared the idea with Irfan?
qa.a: Over lunch last week.

qa.q: How did Aparna feel when Irfan presented the idea?
qa.a: Aparna felt furious and hurt, wanting to scream, then cried in the washroom.

qa.q: What makes Aparna's plan professional rather than reactive?
qa.a: Aparna waited to calm down, got clear on the goal, planned a private talk first, and kept evidence ready if needed.

qa.q: How might Irfan react when Aparna speaks to him privately?
qa.a: Irfan might feel embarrassed and defensive, but a private conversation gives him a chance to put it right.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional managing anger and ego when a colleague takes credit, and planning a calm response.
